We propose a method for precisely measuring the magnitude of a local magnetic field based on atomic interferometry, where a superconducting material serves as the target field source. During an atomic interference experiment, a coherent beam of atoms interferes with itself as it interacts with the superconducting material, and as it passes through a gradient magnetic field, the interference pattern is altered due to the change in field strength. By calculating the change in interference pattern, we can determine the change in the magnetic field strength, and since the superconducting material's response to the Meissner effect provides a precise field source, we can accurately measure the initial magnetic field strength. Additionally, the atomic interference experiment allows for the distinction between changes in the magnetic field caused by local field sources and those caused by overall laboratory frame magnetic fields, thereby enabling the direct measurement of spatial magnetic field gradients. Our calculations indicate that with a rubidium atomic interferometry system, we can measure the change in a local magnetic field at the $10^{-12}$ Tesla level within a second, and with an atomic photon counting system, we can measure spatial magnetic field distributions. Our proposed method provides a means for measuring magnetic field distributions at atomic levels, and our findings suggest that atomic interferometry can complement and bracket magnetic field measurement results obtained with other methods. Our proposed approach also enables the investigation of quantum fluctuations in space-time curvature, the study of magnetic field effects on vacuum entanglement, and the measurement of fundamental constants, which could be achieved by scaling up the atomic interferometry system to use heavier atoms, such as Radium, which would allow for the measurement of extremely weak interactions, including those involving Neutrinos, via the "invisible wall" effect, and the determination of the fine structure constant in atomic units, which could be compared with measurements obtained from atomic spectra and particle scattering experiments. Our proposed method provides a framework for investigating these and other related phenomena. In this work, we examine a mixture model consisting of K components, where the observed data follows an exponential family distribution. This model can be expressed as a weighted sum of the component distributions, with non-negative weights adding up to one. We show that any point in the geometric space defined by this model can be associated with a set of weights representing the relative contributions of each component. This connection enables us to rephrase the task of estimating the weights within the mixture model as a problem of identifying the convex combination of distribution points, subject to certain constraints. We further explore two special cases where the geometric space has a specific structure, namely a line (i.e. a simple mixture) and a plane (i.e. a bimodal mixture). In these scenarios, we can differentiate between the component distributions based on the third-order moments or the curvature of the space defined by the exponential family parameters, offering a means of interpreting the mixture model using Choquet theory. This approach allows us to express the mixture distribution as a function of the underlying data distribution, leveraging the capabilities of Choquet integral in capturing complex patterns of interaction between the component distributions. We also discuss the estimation of the mixture model, focusing on the case where the number of components is unknown. One proposed solution involves an information criterion-based method for determining K, followed by estimation of the weights using the EM algorithm within the specified number of components. We further explore the relationship with existing models such as switching models and activity monitoring models, as well as the connection with Bayesian perspective on mixture modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both simulated and real-world data, comparing our method to existing alternatives and demonstrating the utility of our model in capturing the underlying structure of the data. We also provide a theoretical result concerning the consistency of the proposed estimator under certain conditions. Lastly, we discuss potential applications as well as extensions of our model to other exponential family distributions. One such extension involves incorporating the memory within the activity monitoring model, which we demonstrate using the example of activity monitoring within households. We further outline a roadmap for future research within this framework. We hope that our work will contribute to the integration of statistics and machine learning with geometry and the theory of games, as well as inspire researchers to explore other avenues within the mixture models framework. Concurrent programming on the GPU is increasingly vital for various object-oriented applications, including scientific simulations, that take advantage of multi-threaded computations. Nevertheless, developing and optimizing these applications is complicated due to the limited number of available memory management tools and harsh performance constraints. In response to these challenges, this work presents DynaSOAr, a concurrent memory allocator tailored for object-oriented development on the GPU. DynaSOAr features a novel, object-oriented design that enables users to allocate memory in a way that minimizes performance-critical locking through the use of thread-local pools of pre-allocated memory blocks. In a range of benchmarks and simulations that leverage multi-threaded object-oriented structures, DynaSOAr achieves significant performance improvements over existing GPU memory allocators, often by 1.5 times or more, without requiring a substantial increase in memory usage. Furthermore, DynaSOAr's object-oriented design facilitates seamless integration with existing GPU applications, without the need for a memory allocator rewrite. The developer-friendly API provided by DynaSOAr in addition to its efficient performance makes it an attractive alternative for a broad category of GPU applications that utilize concurrent, object-oriented programming. The allocator's effectiveness is demonstrated across a range of benchmarks including finite element simulations, molecular dynamics simulations, and complicated, real-world applications like OpenFOAM, with performance gains ranging from 1.5 to 5 times over existing GPU memory allocators. The source code for DynaSOAr is openly accessible on GitHub at the link https://github.com/IntelCPL/DynaSOAr. The advice and recommendations presented in this paper can also be applied to the development of other concurrent, object-oriented applications on the GPU. The documentation, tools, and benchmarks used in this work are in addition freely available on the Intel oneAPI Development and Distribution Kit website at the link https://software.intel.com/content/www/us/en/develop/tools/oneapi-base-toolkit.html. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on a superconducting surface. This model, applicable in all relativistic and energy scales, accurately describes the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and provides a clear understanding of their initial principles derivations. By incorporating a harmonic oscillator model, a complete analysis of the YSR states' behavior can be performed, covering local spectral weight, spin polarization, and even lattice displacement effects. To validate this theoretical framework, simulations of Mn adatoms and dimers on a Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with available experimental data, showcasing excellent agreement and offering insights into the effects of vibrational motion and spin-orbit interaction on the YSR states. Additionally, a distinction between YSR state types (zero-bias peaks or valleys) is proposed, based on initial principles derivations, which can be identified by examining the inter-atomic coupling's impact on the YSR states or by positioning the model's center of mass within the superconductor's energy spectrum. A predicted phenomenon of YSR state type switching due to inter-atomic coupling's influence on the magnetic moment distribution is also predicted, which can be experimentally verified using scanning tunneling spectroscopy. A theoretical model of magnetic moment distribution is presented, which can be compared with experimental data and provides a qualitative explanation for the YSR state type switching and offers a novel perspective on the inter-atomic coupling's effect on the YSR states and Kondo lattice models. A discussion on the effects of spin-orbit interaction and vibrational motion on the YSR states is also included, which may have implications for other magnetic impurities on superconducting surfaces. Experimental techniques such as scanning tunneling spectroscopy, low-energy electron diffraction, and Auger electron spectroscopy were used to gather data on Mn adatoms and dimers on a Nb(110) surface, and simulations of this system were conducted using the full relativistic multiple-scattering approach, which provided a detailed understanding of the effects of relativistic effects, inter-atomic coupling, and vibrational motion on the YSR states and offered a visual representation of the magnetic moment distribution, orbital occupation, and local lattice displacement. A comprehensive comparison between the experimental and theoretical results was conducted and new phenomena related to the effects of spin-orbit interaction and vibrational motion on the YSR states and Kondo lattice models were discovered, which may have broader applications to other magnetic impurities on superconducting surfaces. In 1979, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper richness theory within graph theory. They defined an upper rich subgraph as a subgraph without two identical vertices connected by the same number of edges. Our research builds on their work by determining the smallest number, $m$, for which every 2-edge coloring of a countably infinite graph contains an upper rich subgraph of size $m$. We have found that $m$ can be any infinite cardinal greater than 2. We have also explored specific cases, including graphs with an infinite number of components and those without any components at all. Our results in these instances demonstrate the significance of the underlying cardinal characteristics of the graph's vertex set. We have further analyzed the Ramsey theory properties of graphs with an infinite number of components, showing that every infinite graph contains a component that is isomorphic to a specified standard infinite graph, known as an upper rich tree. This finding can be applied to the celebrated Erdos-Gallai theorem and related results. We have also determined the Ramsey upper characteristic of an infinite graph with an infinite number of components to be equal to its cardinal number. Finally, we have explored the upper rich properties of graphs with components of a specific finite size, demonstrating that every finite-sized component contains an upper rich subcomponent of a certain defined size. We have further established that this defined size can be any finite number greater than 2. We have also analyzed the relationship between the size of a component's upper rich subgraph and the number of its elements, deriving a generalization of the Erdos-Gallai theorem. We have also explored the upper rich properties of graphs with components of a specific finite size in a more general context, demonstrating that every component contains a specified defined size of an upper rich subgraph that is itself isomorphic to a specified standard infinite graph, known as an upper rich tree. We have further established that this defined size can be any finite number greater than 2. We have also determined the Ramsey upper characteristic of an infinite graph with a single component to be equal to its cardinal number. A group G has an algebraic diameter of n if its group ring RG has a diameter of n. We are exploring the characteristics of groups with a finite diameter in their ring theory. This work is an addition to the existing research that can be found in the book "Ring Theory". We are examining specific properties of these groups, including how they classify into different categories, the number of groups within each category, and the largest group within each category. Our primary goal is to determine which groups have a finite diameter in their ring theory. This goal is complicated by the fact that the infinite dihidram group does not have a finite diameter, as it is directly constructed from the algebraic diameter of its ring theory. Furthermore, the infinite dihidram group can be used to construct a ring theory with an infinite diameter. We are also examining the relationship between these groups and ask the question of whether there are any finite diameter groups that are not generated from the finite diameter groups that can be derived from their ring theory. Despite its importance, determining the effect of a surface's texture on a fluid's flowability remains challenging due to the intricate relationships between the dimensions of a surface's features, the curvature of the interface between the fluid and the surface, and the resulting texture-induced friction. Doctors often rely on biopsies to diagnose skin cancers, but it's an invasive procedure that may lead to scarring, infections, and emotional distress for patients. A non-invasive method to determine cancer types through an imaging technique called dermoscopy has been developed, but it causes discomfort for long periods of use. To minimize discomfort, it's recommended to reduce the field of view during imaging, which in turn decreases the accuracy of the diagnosis. A deep learning-based method was proposed to accurately identify types of skin cancers from limited dermoscopy images, with an alternate network to detect and exclude outlier samples that may appear in poorly imaged biopsies, based on statistical measures of uncertainty. This method showed significant improvements in diagnosis accuracy for both biopsies with a narrow field of view and those with a full field of view, with an overall accuracy of 94.5% for the former and 93.1% for the latter in a large dataset of images. It also outperformed existing methods in experiments conducted on two smaller dermatology image datasets, with one containing images of skin cancers and the other containing images of moles. The proposed method was named CDN-OULN. Another experiment conducted on a subset of the large dataset of images showed that CDN-OULN can be used to determine whether a biopsy is adequate for an invasive diagnosis, with a high degree of accuracy. The resulting model was termed CancerBiopsyDetector. It has two outputs: one indicating the type of skin cancer and another representing the uncertainty of the prediction, which can be used to determine if the image is of a good quality, with a further analysis of its structure called the entropy of the output layer. The proposed method was tested on three dermoscopy image datasets of skin cancers, with the resulting model trained on two of the datasets and the tests conducted on the third dataset, showing a high level of accuracy even when the images are of a poor quality, with an overall accuracy of 93.5% in one test and 92.3% in another. The ring structure of these derivatives, confirmed by laboratory experiments, allows for a precise understanding of their interstellar chemistry and physics. The ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecules have a long axis aligned with the interstellar magnetic field, suggesting a connection with magnetic field alignment of polar molecules. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that traditional attention mechanisms, although enhancing performance, can lead to target word prediction errors, particularly towards the translation's end. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel look-forward attention mechanism, designed to forecast desired target words in advance and then map the predicted words to the suitable source sentence parts. This forward-thinking attention model allows for not only more efficient processing of complex translations but also better performance on challenging, longer sentence translations. Our results show that this mechanism's significant performance gains, particularly with max-length sentences, are consistent across multiple neural machine translation models and evaluation metrics. Our proposed technique's simplicity and versatile applicability to various models make it a valuable addition to the neural machine translation community. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-MLG-NLPGROUP/Neural-Machine-Translation.

This study examines the long-term behavior of a stochastic process whose duration is defined as the time it takes for a one-dimensional random walk not to return to its initial position within a given time frame. We have derived general expressions for the expected time the process remains above a specific threshold and the probability the process remains above that threshold within a given time frame. These results can be applied to any distribution of step lengths, except those with finite variance. We have also found that as time approaches infinity, the probability the process has not returned to its initial position converges to a constant of 1 minus the square root of the variance of its step length distribution. Additionally, when the step length distribution has a finite second moment, we have derived an explicit expression for this constant. For distributions without a finite second moment, we have established an upper and a lower bound for this constant. Furthermore, we have determined the specific distributions with infinite second moment that result in the process taking an infinitely long time to return to its initial position. We have also established the relationship between the expected time the process remains above a given threshold and a specific parameter that varies slowly over time. This expected time is asymptotically equivalent to the square of this parameter times the time the process remains above this threshold for a single step duration. This finding can be interpreted as the process spending an infinite amount of time near its extreme values. This behavior is not seen for distributions with a finite second moment. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, pinpointing and labeling specific types of nuclei, particularly within crowded tumor samples, proves to be a major challenge. To tackle this issue, a growing number of researchers have turned to using deep learning models, with many current approaches using general object detection algorithms to identify nuclei by drawing on a set of predefined classes. However, locating and labeling individual nuclei can be extremely time-consuming and prone to errors, even for experienced professionals. To automate this process, a more suitable solution involves a more targeted approach, known as nucleus annotation, that only involves identifying and labeling individual nuclei rather than marking tumor areas. Furthermore, this study investigates the robustness of GCNNs, which has not been extensively studied before, and finds that GCNNs are highly resistant to noise. This problem is not unique to Photoshop, as it's common to many other complex software systems, where the lack of accessible algorithm information restricts user creativity and limits potential contributions from the community. In the framework of distributed data processing, the $k$-means clustering algorithm is a fundamental tool that enables independent agents to perform dimensionality reduction on their data. This achievement comes at a cost, as the algorithmic result is disconnected from the underlying data distribution. The problem considered here involves identifying a small set of parameters that characterizes the distribution from which the agents' data are sampled. A new algorithm, known as Harmonic, is presented to solve this problem. It outperforms the existing state-of-the-art algorithm, known as Hubs-and-Spins, in terms of space efficiency, while also achieving a better approximation guarantee when the number of agents is sufficiently large. When the number of agents is vast, this algorithm even approaches the optimal solution, as demonstrated by an lower bound analysis. Additionally, Harmonic yields an improved performance guarantee when the data distribution contains a prominent cluster. This algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness are further illustrated through an experimental comparison with Hubs-and-Spins on real-world datasets. The challenges encountered and the Harmonic algorithm's key components are also discussed in the paper. These difficulties and components include the difficulty of defining a suitable distance metric in high-dimensional data, the difficulty of discovering the underlying data distribution, the difficulty of performing dimensionality reduction, the difficulty of performing approximate inference, and the challenge of defining a suitable quantity to measure the algorithm's performance. The Harmonic algorithm addresses these challenges by utilizing a weighted average of the agents' means, introducing a new renewal reward process, and employing a specific comparison distance metric. The paper's results provide new insights into a previously studied model, known as the Hubs-and-Spins model, as well as a new model, known as the Harmonic model. These models and the Hubs-and-Spins algorithm are also discussed in the paper. The Harmonic algorithm has the potential to be optimized for various models, including the Hubs-and-Spins model, the Harmonic model, the Hubs-and-Spins model with a first-order transition, the Hubs-and-Spins model with a second-order transition, and the Harmonic model with a first-order transition, the Harmonic model with a second-order transition, the model with a large community and small villages, the model with a tree-like structure, and the model with a power-law distribution. The paper concludes by discussing the connections between the Harmonic algorithm and other clustering methods, as well as its potential applications in machine learning. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can significantly
benefit a learner's ability to tackle multiple objectives simultaneously.
However, using a single representation can also result in destructive interference
between tasks, particularly when some tasks are opposing each other.
We introduce a model-based reinforcement learning framework called Modular Systems
Prevent Destructive Interference (MSPDI), which leverages multiple separate representations
to address this interference issue.
By segregating tasks into distinct sub-systems with their own individual representations,
MSPDI avoids inter-system interference and allows for more efficient learning.
We show that a general MSPDI framework can be optimized through a variety of sub-system
configurations, and provide a specific implementation using a modular actor-critic
approach.
Through extensive experiments, we validate MSPDI's effectiveness in resolving destructive
interference in both continuous and discrete action spaces, as well as on both simple
and complex benchmark platforms. 
By analyzing the sub-system configuration's impact on performance, we also observe that
a well-designed MSPDI can even handle opposing objectives by preventing overly destructive
interference, and demonstrate how it can be applied to a real-world problem involving
partially opposing objectives. 
Finally, we conclude by discussing possible future enhancements, including integrating
MSPDI with other reinforcement learning techniques and exploring different sub-system
configurations. 
Our code is available online at https://github.com/ReinforcementLearningAdvancedTopics/2019DeepRPM.

This article examines the possibility of finding invariant surfaces in dynamical systems governed by fractional-order differential equations. To accomplish this goal, we apply the direct method of movers from the calculus of variations to find an invariant surface equation that can be linked to the original dynamical system. Along the way, we encounter an optimization problem involving fractional integrals of differences. By converting this problem into an equivalent form involving the fractional derivative of the difference, we determine the conditions under which an invariant surface does not exist. Specifically, we show that an invariant surface does not exist if the exponent $s$ of the fractional derivative satisfies the condition $s \in (1/2, 1)$. Furthermore, we provide examples of dynamical systems with $s = 1$ that have no invariant surfaces. These results extend and generalize our previous findings, which were limited to the analysis of fractional order systems with the exponent $s=1$. These results also align with the existing research on the possibility of finding invariant surfaces in the corresponding discrete time systems. Additionally, we provide an alternative and simpler proof of the nonexistence of invariant surfaces for the fractional order system with the exponent $s=1$ that utilizes the Banach fixed point theorem. Along the way, we clarify some key assumptions and provide a more detailed analysis of the related optimization problem. To conclude, we offer some final remarks and pose some open research questions related to the possibility of finding invariant surfaces in the mentioned dynamical systems. These questions pertain to the validity of our results for the systems with the exponent $s=1$ when the state space is composed of the discrete points, as well as the possibility of extending our findings to the systems with the changing exponent $s$ over time. These questions also pertain to the possibility of finding invariant surfaces in the mentioned dynamical systems when the possibility of reaching the state $0$ is not guaranteed. To address these research questions, we propose using the suitable Lyapunov functions and the suitable measures of the system's size. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through diluted convolutional layers. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an autoregressive approach with convolutional layers, however, its pitch sensitivity is restricted due to the lack of input frequency selectivity. To overcome this limitation, QPNet introduces a novel architecture that combines the benefits of WN's autoregressive and pitch-sensitive diluted convolutional structures. Specifically, the model employs two types of diluted convolutional layers: one with frequency-selective filters that capture periodic signals like speech, and another with random mask-based convolutional layer that generates stochastic and less periodic signals like breathing sounds. QPNet's combination of these layers enables the generation of highly diverse and complex waveform signals, while significantly reducing the computational burden compared to the full WN model. Experimental evaluations on both speech and polyphonic audio generation demonstrate the improved controllability and diversity of QPNet in comparison to the baseline WN model. This research is applicable to a range of tasks involving the generative modeling of complex and pitch-dependent waveform signals, including speech, polyphonic audio, and medical signal generation. For our approach to locate auditory sources around a moving listener with difficult conditions, we deviate from standard signal processing methods.  We interpret sound source localization as a problem that involves understanding the relationship between a listener's head movements and the varying signals reaching their ears.  To tackle this challenge, we drew inspiration from a category of mathematical functions that describe how signals change during head movements.  We developed a novel method that combines head movement data with time-frequency signal representations.  Our approach allows us to estimate the orientation of the listener's head relative to the sound sources, without relying on reference sounds or specific acoustic environments.  We tested and compared our method against standard approaches using datasets that simulate real-world conditions.  Our results show that our method outperforms the alternatives in various scenarios.  We also explored the role of different signal representations and head movement signals in our method's performance.  Our findings suggest that our approach is particularly effective when sound sources are distant or moving rapidly.  We demonstrated this in further experiments.  We believe our method has potential applications in fields that involve complex acoustic environments and precise head movement tracking.  We ended our evaluation by identifying three such areas.  One of these areas involves the reconstruction of three-dimensional acoustic scenes from raw sound recordings.  Another area involves simulating the effects of head movements and sound scattering on audio signals.  The third area involves the analysis of moving source localization in realistic environments.  We envision further improving our method and expanding its capabilities to tackle these challenges.  To facilitate this, we made our code available to the public.  We also outlined three potential directions for future enhancements.  One potential direction involves integrating our method with existing methods that reconstruct three-dimensional acoustic scenes.  Another direction involves simulating the effects of head movements and sound scattering on audio signals.  The third direction involves analyzing moving source localization in realistic environments.  We described these three directions in more detail.  One of these directions involves integrating our method with existing methods that reconstruct three-dimensional acoustic scenes from raw sound recordings.  We proposed a novel approach to achieve this integration.  Another direction involves simulating the effects of head movements and sound scattering on audio signals.  We described a previous method that achieves this simulation.  The third direction involves analyzing moving source localization in realistic environments.  We proposed a previous method that analyzes this type of scenario.  We also explored the feasibility of integrating our method with a specific previous method that reconstructs three-dimensional acoustic scenes from raw sound recordings.  We demonstrated this in further experiments.

distances. Leveraging the properties of Lorentzian distances, we establish an
analytical expression for the Lorentzian GNN message passing function, which

points. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our LGNN model, which
outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in various challenging real-world
scenarios, including cross-modal applications, graph-based classification, and

Specifically, we're investigating a scenario in which an unknown, rigid body is positioned inside an acoustic chamber and we're attempting to recover the object's shape, size, and position based solely on measurements of the chamber's sound waves emitted during a vibration test. By assuming the object has a specific, known structure, we can leverage a computational method called a level set structural optimization technique to approximate its properties. A numerical example using a 2D acoustic chamber demonstrates that the object's characteristics can be successfully reconstructed when its size is fixed, although difficulties arise when its size is unknown. Similarly, positioning the object is also achievable, but more challenging conditions lead to less accurate results. A comparative analysis highlights the effectiveness of using different sensors and the chamber's object-filled scenario, whereas a further example illustrates the approach's applicability to real-world scenarios with unknown space dimensions. A novel adaptation of the method, designed to handle outside vibration data, enables the successful reconstruction of an object within a freely accessible space. We have undertaken a comprehensive review of harmonic gauge theories in the context of significant gravity models. Our exploration encompasses variations of the harmonic gauge condition and associated development of the perturbative expansion, which we have made readily accessible in an easily usable format. Our analysis also delves into the intricacies of the harmonic gauge in the significant gravity framework, specifically within the Weyl and self-dual gravity paradigms. Furthermore, our study examines the occurrence of harmonic gauge choices that lead to odd-odd perturbative expansions, which we believe presents a novel finding in the field. Our research aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion regarding the choice of harmonic gauge condition and to provide an in-depth analysis of specific examples that can be useful for a broader gravitational physics community. Our work is also intended to serve as a starting point for further exploration of key issues in the field. Our review has been conducted in a way that allows each section to be studied independently, which we believe will be beneficial for a wide range of researchers with diverse interests. Our study has further implications for the implications of harmonic gauge theories on black hole physics and the cosmological background. Our review has been accompanied by a list of relevant open-source code that can be used for educational purposes by undergraduate students. Our research has also been presented at the 19th Asian Pacific Physics Meeting, held in Busan, Korea, from 25 to 29 July 2022, under the session name "Physics of Black Holes and Cosmology". Our work on harmonic gauge theories in the context of significant gravity models will continue in the future, with our immediate plans being to investigate the occurrence of ghost fields in these models. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been successfully applied within the framework of the Gibbs distribution, yielding intriguing results that extend beyond its initial theoretical proof. This approach has led to optimized objectives that can be tailored to suit various statistical systems and their corresponding operators. In the course of our analysis, we derive a key parameter, $x_0$, which marks the threshold above which negative temperatures become relevant. Our primary focus on the statistical systems themselves allows us to provide a more precise interpretation of the optimized expectations, including a mean energy value that can even be determined for a specific quadratic system. Furthermore, we establish that the most recent negativity indicator, based on the spread of the system's energy distribution, is equivalent to the overlap between this distribution and a step function. In the process, we demonstrate that this indicator can be expressed in terms of the system's total energy and the $x_0$ parameter, which enables us to determine the specific conditions under which a system's energy distribution is considered negative. Our study also explores the relationship between the average energy and the number of systems, revealing that the average energy remains independent of the system's size, and that it must exceed the $x_0$ threshold in order to be considered negative. Our research further expands on this concept by investigating a quadratic system with a finite number of systems, and demonstrates that the most recent negativity indicator is not only capable of detecting the presence of negative temperature in any given system, but it can also determine the specific systems that possess a negative temperature. Our analysis also leads to an interesting finding regarding the distribution of systems at a negative temperature, which turns out to be a geometric distribution. The number of chest X-ray images being collected and stored digitally has been escalating in recent years. While this abundance of data has been beneficial for training artificial neural networks, it also raises concerns about complying with patient privacy laws and HIPAA regulations. Additionally, as medical institutions share and collaborate more closely, there's a growing need to anonymize patient data, including X-rays. In response to these challenges, researchers have been exploring methods to intentionally degrade chest X-rays while minimizing the impact on artificial neural networks used for illness detection. However, evaluating these methods presents a significant obstacle in the form of a lack of suitable datasets with corresponding score and image files, making it difficult to Reproduce and verify these results. In an attempt to address this issue, the authors have created a new dataset comprising 600 chest X-ray images that have been degraded at three different levels and paired with corresponding masks highlighting the affected areas. This new dataset is tailored for evaluating and refining image restoration techniques with an eye on developing more effective methods to securely share and collaborate on chest X-ray data. Experimental results indicate that employing a combination of Fourier transform and progressive transformation techniques leads to the development of a simple yet highly reliable model for refining artificial neural networks trained on low-quality images, with a performance gap of just 1.3% compared to the high-quality version. This model can restore images at various degradation levels and exhibits a strong relationship with the Fourier transform of noise. Furthermore, this model has been integrated into a system for securely sharing and collaborating on chest X-ray data via an anonymous platform called MedNISP, along with an accompanying discussion on implementation details and future research possibilities. This work has been deposited in the open-domain repository arXiv with the identifier 2203.05378. In the course of analyzing lung X-ray images, researchers encountered difficulties in establishing a reliable quantitative indicator to evaluate the distortion's impact on neural networks used for illness detection. As a result, they employed a straightforward yet effective approach based on a fixed artificial neural network to assess the distortion's influence, with the network's performance on an normal image serving as a baseline. Any decrease in performance was attributed to the impact of the distortion. Additionally, they discovered that the influence of the distortion varied greatly depending on the image, with some images experiencing a minimal impact, while others were affected more significantly. To rectify this issue, they proposed an innovative approach involving the training of a separate artificial neural network for each individual image, with the network's primary purpose being to determine whether the image in question is normal or ill.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data analysis, specifically designed for expert technicians who need a quick and intuitive approach to visualize and investigate high-speed measurement data in industrial settings. The tool can handle large datasets of up to 64 parameters across 32 devices, with measurements taken at high frequencies of up to 100 Hz for each device. These measurements are represented as 3D vectors in a 3D space defined by x, y, and theta axes, allowing for in-depth analysis of data patterns, oscillations, and other anomalies. With features like real-time visualization, historical plotting, and advanced signal processing, ViDaExpert enables rapid diagnosis and optimization of industrial processes. The application forms part of a larger framework that includes a development kit (DK) for creating customized applications, and is suitable for use in a variety of industrial contexts, including power generation, manufacturing, and automotive sectors.
